## http.exposure.sensitive_path

**Sensitive file is publicly readable** · active · default severity **high**

The web server serves a file that should never be public: /.git/HEAD means the whole Git repository (source code and history, often with credentials) can be downloaded, and /.env usually holds database passwords and API keys. Seta reads only these files and reports variable names, never values.

**How to fix:** Deny access to dotfiles in the web server (e.g. nginx "location ~ /\. { deny all; }"), deploy without the .git directory, and rotate every secret the exposed files contained.

**References:**

- <https://owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/latest/4-Web_Application_Security_Testing/02-Configuration_and_Deployment_Management_Testing/04-Review_Old_Backup_and_Unreferenced_Files_for_Sensitive_Information>

## http.headers.csp_missing

**No Content-Security-Policy** · passive · default severity **low**

The page sets no Content-Security-Policy, so a single cross-site scripting bug lets an attacker run any script and load it from anywhere. A report-only policy doesn't count.

**How to fix:** Add a Content-Security-Policy header. Start with Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only to find what the page loads, then enforce a policy such as "default-src 'self'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'".

**References:**

- <https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Content-Security-Policy>
- <https://www.w3.org/TR/CSP3/>

## http.headers.frame_protection_missing

**Page can be framed by other sites** · passive · default severity **low**

The page sets neither X-Frame-Options nor a CSP frame-ancestors directive, so any site can embed it in a frame and trick visitors into clicking on it (clickjacking).

**How to fix:** Send "Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self'" (or 'none'), or "X-Frame-Options: DENY" for older browsers.

**References:**

- <https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/X-Frame-Options>
- <https://owasp.org/www-community/attacks/Clickjacking>

## http.headers.nosniff_missing

**No X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff** · passive · default severity **low**

Without "X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff", browsers may guess a response's type from its content, so an uploaded file served as text can be executed as script or style.

**How to fix:** Send "X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff" on every response.

**References:**

- <https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/X-Content-Type-Options>

## http.headers.referrer_policy_missing

**No Referrer-Policy** · passive · default severity **info**

The page sets no Referrer-Policy. Current browsers default to strict-origin-when-cross-origin, but older ones send full URLs, including paths and query strings, to every site the page links to.

**How to fix:** Send "Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin" (or stricter).

**References:**

- <https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Referrer-Policy>

## http.hsts.missing

**No HSTS header** · passive · default severity **medium**

The host's HTTPS responses have no Strict-Transport-Security header, so browsers will keep trying plain HTTP first, and an attacker on the network can strip the redirect to HTTPS.

**How to fix:** Send "Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains" on every HTTPS response once the whole site works over HTTPS.

**References:**

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6797>
- <https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Strict-Transport-Security>

## http.hsts.preload_not_ready

**HSTS asks for preloading but doesn't qualify** · passive · default severity **low**

The domain's HSTS header carries the preload directive, but the domain doesn't meet the requirements of the browsers' HSTS preload list (max-age of at least a year, includeSubDomains, and an HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect on the same host), so a preload submission would be rejected.

**How to fix:** Serve "Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload" on the apex domain and redirect http:// to https:// on the same host first, or drop the preload directive.

**References:**

- <https://hstspreload.org/#submission-requirements>

## http.hsts.weak

**HSTS header is invalid or short-lived** · passive · default severity **low**

The Strict-Transport-Security header is malformed, or its max-age is under 180 days, so browsers forget it quickly and returning visitors are exposed to HTTPS stripping again. max-age=0 turns HSTS off.

**How to fix:** Use a max-age of at least 15552000 (180 days); 31536000 (a year) is the common choice.

**References:**

- <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6797#section-6.1>

## http.redirect.missing

**HTTP doesn't redirect to HTTPS** · passive · default severity **medium**

The host answers plain-HTTP requests on port 80 without redirecting them to HTTPS, so visitors who type the bare name or follow an old http:// link use an unencrypted connection that anyone on the network can read and modify.

**How to fix:** Answer every request on port 80 with a 301 (or 308) redirect to the same URL over https://.

**References:**

- <https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Security/Practical_implementation_guides/TLS#http_redirections>
